discussion.title: RFC: Scout 2.0 Architecture Pivot — From Issue Tracker to Agentic Context Engine
discussion.body:
> **👋 Note to Reviewers:**
> We are pivoting Scout from a simple issue tracker into a platform-agnostic Agentic Context Engine (using MCP). I am looking for community feedback on:
> 1. The `STATE.md` handoff system (Are there edge cases we missed when switching IDEs manually?)
> 2. The DB Schema for generalizing Jira/Linear/GitHub tasks.
> 3. Token optimization via dynamic skill loading.
> 
> Please poke holes in this architecture!

# Scout: The Agentic Context Engine
## Technical & UX Architecture

---

## What Scout Will Become

Scout is no longer just an issue tracker. It is an **Agentic Context Engine** — a platform that:

1. Collects tasks from any source (GitHub, Jira, Linear)
2. Lets the user manage and prioritise them in a beautiful dashboard
3. When the user says "Solve", Scout **orchestrates** the AI by feeding it the right context and skills via MCP
4. The AI (Antigravity, Cursor, Copilot) does the actual coding
5. Scout tracks progress and closes the loop

---

## The Complete End-to-End Flow

    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                     CLOUD (Scout Dashboard)                     │
    │                                                                 │
    │  GitHub Issues ──┐                                              │
    │  Jira Tickets  ──┼──► Scout Database (Supabase)                 │
    │  Linear Issues ──┘         │                                    │
    │                            │  User sees unified task queue      │
    │                            │  User clicks "Solve" on a task     │
    └────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┘
                                 │
                                 │ (Scout shows setup instructions)
                                 │
    ┌────────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                   LOCAL MACHINE (User's Laptop)                 │
    │                                                                 │
    │  1. User clones the target repo                                 │
    │     git clone https://github.com/org/repo                      │
    │                                                                 │
    │  2. Scout MCP server is running (installed once, runs always)   │
    │     Connected to Scout's cloud via user's credentials           │
    │                                                                 │
    │  3. Scout Skills live inside the repo                           │
    │     repo/.scout/skills/                                         │
    │       ├── scout-planner/SKILL.md                                │
    │       ├── scout-proof-fix/SKILL.md                              │
    │       ├── scout-run-tests/SKILL.md                              │
    │       └── ...                                                   │
    │                                                                 │
    │  4. User opens IDE (Antigravity / Cursor / Copilot)             │
    │     Says: "Solve issue #123 from Scout"                         │
    │                                                                 │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                 │
                                 ▼
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                  SCOUT MCP ORCHESTRATION LOOP                   │
    │                                                                 │
    │  STEP 1 — ANALYSE (Scout → AI)                                  │
    │  Scout MCP calls: get_task_blueprint(task_id)                   │
    │  Returns to AI:                                                 │
    │    "Here is the full issue. Here is the repo context.           │
    │     Your first job: READ this. Then tell me what TYPE           │
    │     of problem this is: bug_fix / new_feature / docs..."        │
    │                                                                 │
    │  ↓ AI reads the issue, reads relevant code files                │
    │  ↓ AI classifies: "This is a bug_fix"                           │
    │  ↓ AI calls Scout MCP: report_analysis(type="bug_fix")          │
    │                                                                 │
    │  STEP 2 — SKILL SELECTION (Scout decides)                       │
    │  Scout receives the classification from the AI.                 │
    │  Scout looks up the skill map for "bug_fix".                    │
    │  Scout reads relevant SKILL.md files from the local repo.       │
    │  Scout returns them to the AI as the execution instructions.    │
    │                                                                 │
    │  STEP 3 — EXECUTION (AI follows skills)                         │
    │  AI now has clear, step-by-step skill instructions.             │
    │  It plans → codes → proves the fix → runs tests → reviews.     │
    │                                                                 │
    │  STEP 4 — COMPLETION (AI → Scout)                               │
    │  AI opens a Pull Request.                                       │
    │  AI calls: mark_task_status(task_id, "pr_opened", pr_url)       │
    │  Scout updates the cloud dashboard automatically.               │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

---

## Why the AI Does the Analysis (Not Scout)

The AI that is already in the user's IDE does the analysis as **Step 1 of the skill workflow**. 

**Why this is better:**
- No extra API costs — the same AI session that solves the issue also classifies it.
- The AI reads actual code, not just the title — it can tell a bug from a feature by looking at the failing test or the missing function.
- No latency from a cloud round-trip — it happens instantly in the local IDE session.
- Scout stays simple — it is the conductor, not the analyst.

---

## Scout Skills System & Token Optimisation

Skills are `SKILL.md` files stored directly inside the target repository under `.scout/skills/`. They travel with the repo — any developer who clones the project and connects Scout MCP gets the skills automatically.

Scout only loads the skills relevant to the issue type. This keeps token usage low.

| Issue Type | Skills Loaded | Approx Tokens |
|---|---|---|
| **Bug Fix** | planner + proof-fix + run-tests + adversarial-review | ~2,000 |
| **New Feature** | planner + tamper-guard + run-tests | ~1,500 |
| **Performance** | planner + proof-fix + run-tests + honest-stop | ~1,800 |
| **Security** | planner + tamper-guard + adversarial-review + honest-stop | ~2,000 |
| **Documentation** | planner + honest-stop | ~800 |
| **Refactor** | planner + tamper-guard + run-tests + adversarial-review | ~2,000 |

**Without this system:** Every task would load all skills = ~4,500 tokens every time.  
**With this system:** Tasks load only what they need = 800–2,000 tokens per task.  
**Token savings: up to 55–80% reduction.**

---

## State Persistence & Model Switching (The "Handoff" System)

A critical requirement is the ability to **switch AI models mid-task**. For example, if a user hits their IDE token limit, they should be able to switch to another IDE without the new AI having to re-read the issue, re-plan the task, or lose track of what was already done.

Scout will use a **filesystem-based state checkpointing system**:

1. **The `STATE.md` File**: When the AI begins a task, it creates or updates a `.scout/STATE.md` file in the root of the local repository. 
2. **Continuous Checkpointing**: The AI is instructed via the `scout-planner` skill to write its plan to `STATE.md` and mark checkboxes (`[x]`) as it completes each step. It must also log the current `task_id`.
3. **The Interruption**: AI runs out of tokens while halfway through fixing a bug. The IDE stops.
4. **The Handoff**: The user opens another IDE in the same repository and prompts: *"Resume my Scout task."*
5. **The Resumption**: Because `STATE.md` is a plain text markdown file, the new IDE reads it immediately. It sees the `task_id`, sees which steps are checked off, and resumes on the exact unchecked step where the previous IDE failed.

By storing the execution state in the local filesystem (`.scout/STATE.md`), **any IDE and any AI model can natively read it**. The state travels with the code.

---

## Scout MCP Server

### Location in Monorepo
```text
Open_Source_Scout/
  packages/
    scout-mcp/
      src/
        index.ts          ← MCP server entry point
        auth.ts           ← reads ~/.scout/credentials.json
        skills-loader.ts  ← reads SKILL.md files from local repo
        tools/
          get_assigned_tasks.ts
          get_task_blueprint.ts
          report_analysis.ts
          mark_task_status.ts

discussion.body:
### 🏷️ Discussion Type

Product Feedback

### Body

Hey everyone, I am pivoting my open-source project, Scout, into an Agentic Context Engine that feeds Jira/Linear tasks into local AI IDEs via the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

I just wrote a massive technical architecture report and would love feedback from any open-source builders here. Specifically looking for edge cases on how we handle manual AI Model handoffs via a local STATE.md file.

Read the full RFC and drop your thoughts here: https://github.com/Rahul-pamula/Open_Source_Scout/issues/187

### Guidelines

- [X] I have read and understood this category's [guidelines](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/51384) before making this post.

    │  2. Scout MCP server is running (installed once, runs always)   │
    │     Connected to Scout's cloud via user's credentials           │
    │                                                                 │
    │  3. Scout Skills live inside the repo                           │
    │     repo/.scout/skills/                                         │
    │       ├── scout-planner/SKILL.md                                │
    │       ├── scout-proof-fix/SKILL.md                              │
    │       ├── scout-run-tests/SKILL.md                              │
    │       └── ...                                                   │
    │                                                                 │
    │  4. User opens IDE (Antigravity / Cursor / Copilot)             │
    │     Says: "Solve issue #123 from Scout"                         │
    │                                                                 │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                 │
                                 ▼
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                  SCOUT MCP ORCHESTRATION LOOP                   │
    │                                                                 │
    │  STEP 1 — ANALYSE (Scout → AI)                                  │
    │  Scout MCP calls: get_task_blueprint(task_id)                   │
    │  Returns to AI:                                                 │
    │    "Here is the full issue. Here is the repo context.           │
    │     Your first job: READ this. Then tell me what TYPE           │
    │     of problem this is: bug_fix / new_feature / docs..."        │
    │                                                                 │
    │  ↓ AI reads the issue, reads relevant code files                │
    │  ↓ AI classifies: "This is a bug_fix"                           │
    │  ↓ AI calls Scout MCP: report_analysis(type="bug_fix")          │
    │                                                                 │
    │  STEP 2 — SKILL SELECTION (Scout decides)                       │
    │  Scout receives the classification from the AI.                 │
    │  Scout looks up the skill map for "bug_fix".                    │
    │  Scout reads relevant SKILL.md files from the local repo.       │
    │  Scout returns them to the AI as the execution instructions.    │
    │                                                                 │
    │  STEP 3 — EXECUTION (AI follows skills)                         │
    │  AI now has clear, step-by-step skill instructions.             │
    │  It plans → codes → proves the fix → runs tests → reviews.     │
    │                                                                 │
    │  STEP 4 — COMPLETION (AI → Scout)                               │
    │  AI opens a Pull Request.                                       │
    │  AI calls: mark_task_status(task_id, "pr_opened", pr_url)       │
    │  Scout updates the cloud dashboard automatically.               │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

---

## Why the AI Does the Analysis (Not Scout)

The AI that is already in the user's IDE does the analysis as **Step 1 of the skill workflow**. 

**Why this is better:**
- No extra API costs — the same AI session that solves the issue also classifies it.
- The AI reads actual code, not just the title — it can tell a bug from a feature by looking at the failing test or the missing function.
- No latency from a cloud round-trip — it happens instantly in the local IDE session.
- Scout stays simple — it is the conductor, not the analyst.

---

## Scout Skills System & Token Optimisation

Skills are `SKILL.md` files stored directly inside the target repository under `.scout/skills/`. They travel with the repo — any developer who clones the project and connects Scout MCP gets the skills automatically.

Scout only loads the skills relevant to the issue type. This keeps token usage low.

| Issue Type | Skills Loaded | Approx Tokens |
|---|---|---|
| **Bug Fix** | planner + proof-fix + run-tests + adversarial-review | ~2,000 |
| **New Feature** | planner + tamper-guard + run-tests | ~1,500 |
| **Performance** | planner + proof-fix + run-tests + honest-stop | ~1,800 |
| **Security** | planner + tamper-guard + adversarial-review + honest-stop | ~2,000 |
| **Documentation** | planner + honest-stop | ~800 |
| **Refactor** | planner + tamper-guard + run-tests + adversarial-review | ~2,000 |

**Without this system:** Every task would load all skills = ~4,500 tokens every time.  
**With this system:** Tasks load only what they need = 800–2,000 tokens per task.  
**Token savings: up to 55–80% reduction.**

---

## State Persistence & Model Switching (The "Handoff" System)

A critical requirement is the ability to **switch AI models mid-task**. For example, if a user hits their IDE token limit, they should be able to switch to another IDE without the new AI having to re-read the issue, re-plan the task, or lose track of what was already done.

Scout will use a **filesystem-based state checkpointing system**:

1. **The `STATE.md` File**: When the AI begins a task, it creates or updates a `.scout/STATE.md` file in the root of the local repository. 
2. **Continuous Checkpointing**: The AI is instructed via the `scout-planner` skill to write its plan to `STATE.md` and mark checkboxes (`[x]`) as it completes each step. It must also log the current `task_id`.
3. **The Interruption**: AI runs out of tokens while halfway through fixing a bug. The IDE stops.
4. **The Handoff**: The user opens another IDE in the same repository and prompts: *"Resume my Scout task."*
5. **The Resumption**: Because `STATE.md` is a plain text markdown file, the new IDE reads it immediately. It sees the `task_id`, sees which steps are checked off, and resumes on the exact unchecked step where the previous IDE failed.

By storing the execution state in the local filesystem (`.scout/STATE.md`), **any IDE and any AI model can natively read it**. The state travels with the code.

---

## Scout MCP Server

### Location in Monorepo
```text
Open_Source_Scout/
  packages/
    scout-mcp/
      src/
        index.ts          ← MCP server entry point
        auth.ts           ← reads ~/.scout/credentials.json
        skills-loader.ts  ← reads SKILL.md files from local repo
        tools/
          get_assigned_tasks.ts
          get_task_blueprint.ts
          report_analysis.ts
          mark_task_status.ts
